ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study protocol was approved by the Kaiser Permanente Interregional Institutional Review Board (IRB), as well as the IRBs of Emory University and Boston University (IRB# 2130008).
To minimize recall bias, participants were excluded from the study if they did not respond within six days of receiving the recruitment email.
table.header: AGE and ARI case definition, recruitment, and eligibility criteria

table.text: Participants were asked to report contacts lasting more than five minutes to focus on substantive social interactions (7, 29, 30), reduce potential recall error from brief incidental encounters (31), and minimize response burden among acutely ill participants (Supplementary Methods).
table.formatted: Participants were asked to report contacts lasting more than five minutes to focus on substantive social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">30)</ref>, reduce potential recall error from brief incidental encounters <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(31)</ref>, and minimize response burden among acutely ill participants (Supplementary Methods).
table.header: Surveys for AGE and ARI cases

table.text: We excluded respondents who reported more than 20 contacts at home or more than 250 contacts at work, school, or other community settings because such large numbers were deemed implausible given that participants were only asked to report physical, conversational or close-proximity contacts lasting more than five minutes.

For each stratum defined by sex, age group, and disease type, the post-stratification weight was calculated as the ratio of the number of medically attended cases in the MarketScan/Medicare database to the corresponding number of participants enrolled in the SickMix study.
Electronic informed consent was obtained from adult participants through an online form prior to survey participation.
Our participants generally reported a higher number of contacts than participants in previous social contact studies, even when they were sick.
Also, because we recruited individuals who were actively ill, we minimized participant burden by simplifying and shortening the survey.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> To minimize recall bias, participants were excluded from the study if they did not respond within six days of receiving the recruitment email.

> Participants were asked to report contacts lasting more than five minutes to focus on substantive social interactions (7, 29, 30), reduce potential recall error from brief incidental encounters (31), and minimize response burden among acutely ill participants (Supplementary Methods).

> We excluded respondents who reported more than 20 contacts at home or more than 250 contacts at work, school, or other community settings because such large numbers were deemed implausible given that participants were only asked to report physical, conversational or close-proximity contacts lasting more than five minutes.

> For each stratum defined by sex, age group, and disease type, the post-stratification weight was calculated as the ratio of the number of medically attended cases in the MarketScan/Medicare database to the corresponding number of participants enrolled in the SickMix study.

> Electronic informed consent was obtained from adult participants through an online form prior to survey participation.

> Our participants generally reported a higher number of contacts than participants in previous social contact studies, even when they were sick.

> Also, because we recruited individuals who were actively ill, we minimized participant burden by simplifying and shortening the survey.

Ethics approval statement:

> The study protocol was approved by the Kaiser Permanente Interregional Institutional Review Board (IRB), as well as the IRBs of Emory University and Boston University (IRB# 2130008).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

#### Descriptives Overview

We found 0 columns with at least one missing value.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 42 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified
4 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("cases_1week_matrix.xlsx", "cases_2week_matrix.xlsx", "cases_index_home_matrix.xlsx", "cases_index_matrix.xlsx"), Column = c("<1", "<1", "<1", "<1"), Issues = c("🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\"<\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\"<\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\"<\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\"<\")" )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.
